messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Amir

Amir was fifty-six when the police officer's baton struck him across the ribs. He had been standing on the sidewalk outside a community center in his neighborhood, speaking with a friend about the upcoming city council meeting, when a protest two blocks away had turned chaotic. Officers in riot gear swept through the street indiscriminately. Amir raised his hands, tried to move away, but the officer—a man whose face he would never see clearly—had already decided. The blow came without warning. He fell hard, tasted blood mixed with the copper of his own fillings, felt the officer's boot press against his shoulder as more impacts landed. His friend screamed. The officer called him names. Within minutes it was over, but Amir lay there gasping, his ribs on fire, and a certainty had crystallized in him: the world had shown its true face, and it was indifferent to justice or innocence.

For weeks afterward, Amir tried to convince himself it was an isolated incident, a terrible mistake. But the conviction had taken root too deeply. He began to see threat everywhere. Walking to his car in the parking garage at work, he found himself mapping exits before he even reached his desk—which stairwell was closest, whether the elevator could trap him. At stoplights, he scanned the sidewalk for uniforms, for sudden movement. His wife, Leila, noticed him tensing at the sound of sirens. He could not relax, even in their living room with the doors locked, the lights on, Leila beside him. Some part of his mind remained on high alert, convinced that safety was an illusion, that people—especially those in authority—were not what they seemed. They had their own agendas, their own capacity for violence. Trust was a luxury he could no longer afford.

What frightened him most was his own rage. When the memory surfaced—and it surfaced constantly, unbidden, in fragments—he felt a fury so intense it terrified him. The taste of blood would return, metallic and immediate, and with it came a white-hot anger at himself, at the officer, at a system that had violated something fundamental in him. He had always been a measured man, thoughtful, the kind of person who believed in dialogue and understanding. Now he was someone capable of fantasizing about retaliation, about violence. This contradiction between who he believed himself to be and what he felt capable of had shattered something in his self-image. He had acted—or wanted to act—in ways that went against everything he valued. The shame of that desire was almost worse than the physical pain.

To manage the unbearable tightness in his chest, the constant vigilance, the rage that erupted without warning, Amir began to withdraw. He stopped watching news programs, deleted social media apps from his phone, avoided any content that might remind him of what had happened. He told himself these were reasonable precautions. But the avoidance extended further. He stopped allowing himself to feel anything at all if he could help it. He declined invitations from friends. He became mechanical at work, responding to client emails with minimal engagement, avoiding the creative brainstorming sessions that had once energized him. Leila tried to draw him into conversation, but he found himself shutting down, unable to risk the vulnerability of connection. His belief that people were fundamentally untrustworthy made intimacy feel dangerous. If he let her close, if he allowed himself to feel anything—love, hope, even ordinary happiness—he risked being hurt again. Better to feel nothing.

Yet the very strategies meant to protect him were keeping the memory alive. By avoiding anything that might trigger emotion, by constantly scanning his surroundings, by refusing to fully process what had happened, he had frozen the trauma in place. When memories did break through—and they did, despite his vigilance—he would push them away before they could fully surface, cutting himself off mid-recollection, as though incompleteness might diminish their power. It never did. The fragmented images, the taste, the rage, they all returned more insistently. His conviction that the world was inherently dangerous, that people could not be trusted, that he himself was capable of unthinkable things—these beliefs only deepened as he isolated himself further, as each avoided situation seemed to confirm his worst fears.

After six months of this, Leila finally insisted he see someone. Amir resisted, certain that talking would only make things worse, that a therapist would judge him for the violent thoughts he harbored, that opening up would expose him to more pain. But he was exhausted. The vigilance, the emotional numbness, the fractured memory that would not release him—it was unsustainable. He came to his first appointment reluctant and afraid, convinced that his world had fundamentally changed and that he could never truly be safe again.
